title: The F2 exposure window shrinks twice as fast per rating point as the F1 window
content:
The two threshold functions in the reference implementation differ in both anchor and slope:

```
f1_thresholds_low_risk:  x_start = (50 - rating) * 0.01
f2_thresholds_high_risk: x_start = (75 - rating) * 0.02
```

matching the parameter sets at A.3.2.2.1.2.3.3.1.5.4.1 (i = 0.01, r_i = 50) and A.3.2.2.1.2.3.3.1.5.4.2 (i = 0.02, r_i = 75).

Each anchor is the top of the band the ratio governs — 50 is the ceiling of Medium risk, above which F1 stops being used; 75 is the ceiling of High risk, above which the charge is automatically 100%. Both windows therefore close exactly where their regime ends, which is a coherent choice rather than two unrelated calibrations.

The slopes are not symmetric, though, and the reason is that the two ratios are denominated differently. F1 is exposure beyond ecosystem risk capital as a fraction of *total system debt* — a number that is small in normal conditions, so a 1%-per-point scale spreads the response across a plausible range. F2 is the Agent's own exposure over its *own Total Risk Capital* — a number that can easily exceed 1, so tolerance is consumed twice as fast per rating point.

The practical implication is that the same rating change means something quite different depending on which band a protocol sits in. Moving a protocol from rating 40 to 45 shifts its F1 allowance by 5 points of system debt; moving one from 60 to 65 shifts its F2 allowance by 10 points of the Agent's risk capital. Rating precision matters more, in capital terms, at the risky end — which is the opposite of where the framework's inputs (audit coverage tiers, TVL logarithms, complexity proxies) are most reliable.
description: F1 uses 1% of allowance per rating point measured against total system debt; F2 uses 2% per point against the Agent's own risk capital, both anchored at the top of their applicable risk bands.
